idiom_name: shared no-op implementation of the collaborator interface (usually a singleton)
implementation_notes: Define the collaborator interface once and add a second implementation whose methods produce neutral results - no-op for commands and identity/empty/false/zero for queries - then make that instance shared and immutable and install it wherever the real collaborator may be absent (constructor default, factory fallback, dependency-injection default), so callers receive a reference that is never null and drop their guards. The neutral implementation must satisfy the interface's contract, not just its signature: if a method promises an effect (persist, send, charge), a no-op version breaks substitutability and the collaboration needs an option value or a real special case instead.
pitfalls: Subclassing the real implementation instead of implementing the interface silently inherits real behaviour for every method added later.
Giving the null instance mutable state turns it into shared global state and makes 'neutral' behaviour order-dependent.
Using the null object where absence must be observable (audit, authorisation, persistence) converts a wiring failure into silent success.

Wrong move: use a Null Object to turn a failed lookup or invalid input into a harmless default -> downstream work continues with misleading state and the original error can disappear -> instead return Option/Result or fail at the boundary, reserving Null Objects for benign absence.
sources: Woolf, Bobby: 'The Null Object Pattern' (PLoP '96), published as 'Null Object' in R. Martin, F. Buschmann & D. Riehle (eds.), Pattern Languages of Program Design 3, Addison-Wesley, 1998, pp. 5-18.
